questions.prompt: DESIGN IT — [senior] keeping the outbox fair and finite when one tenant floods it (organized-study-support-desk-crm, docs/features/003-outbox-worker-notifications.md). Scenario: a tenant migrating from its old help desk replays eight years of history through the API one evening, emitting about 250,000 outbox events in four hours, many of them repeated updates to the same tickets; the other 119 tenants' agents keep working, and their customers expect a reply email within two minutes; nothing has ever been deleted from the outbox table, which is nearing 10 million rows. Write your design before you look: how work is shared so the flood cannot starve the other tenants, which of the flood's events should be collapsed, rolled into a digest or never sent at all, what the worker's query needs from the schema once it picks per tenant, what a 10-million-row table does to that query and to every status change, and what happens to a row after it has been sent. Then tick the checkpoints you covered and add up the weights (suggested pass: 70% with every [w3] hit)

keyPoints.text: [w3] Separate classes of work before doing any fairness arithmetic: a customer waiting on a reply email is interactive, an import's replayed history is bulk. Give the reply topic its own lane, or strict priority over bulk topics, so no volume of bulk rows can ever sit in front of it; every row already carries a topic and a tenant, so the split is a predicate, not a new table.

[w3] Inside a lane, share by tenant: rotate over the tenants that have pending rows (a weighted or deficit round robin), taking at most a handful per tenant on each pass, so the importer drains at its share while the other 119 see an almost empty queue. Today a pass is a single global slice of the oldest pending rows, so whoever enqueued most decides what goes out next.

[w2] The schema does not yet serve a per-tenant pick: the outbox is indexed on (status, createdAt) and on (tenantId, topic), and 'this tenant's oldest pending rows' matches neither. Add (tenantId, status, createdAt), or a partial index over pending rows only, before switching the poller, and the same index answers the oldest-pending-age-per-tenant metric that proves fairness works.

[w3] The cheapest event is the one never sent: replayed history must not email customers about tickets closed years ago. Producers emit unconditionally today (a public reply always gets its notification row), so the import needs a mode that still writes the change and its audit row but marks its events as not customer-facing, and a ticket touched 40 times by the import should collapse to its latest state, which the sender can read when it sends.

[w2] Ten million rows do not by themselves slow the pending lookup: while it matches (status, createdAt) it reads a narrow index range. What hurts is churn: each event is written three times (insert, PROCESSING with an attempt count, PROCESSED with a time) and each status change rewrites an indexed column, so a quarter-million-event evening leaves dead row versions and dead index entries that vacuum must keep up with.

[w2] Sent rows must leave: no code anywhere deletes an outbox row, so the table is both queue and history. Once a row is PROCESSED with its processed time, it is only a delivery record: delete it after a retention period in small batches, move it to an archive table, or partition by creation time and drop whole old partitions, the cheapest delete at this size.

questions.prompt: PRE-MORTEM — the redesign, three weeks in: delivery is now ordered per tenant, and one tenant's notifications have not moved since an email template began throwing on a single malformed event; a deploy started the nightly digest job twice and some customers received the same digest twice; after retries with backoff were added, every pass got slower week by week although the pending count stayed small; the cleanup job that deletes sent rows makes the database crawl at midnight; and the importer's own backlog keeps paging on-call all evening. What breaks, how would you notice, and what is the repair?

keyPoints.text: [w3] Strict per-tenant ordering turns one poison row into a frozen tenant: everything behind the first event that always fails waits for it. Today a throwing event is merely marked FAILED and the pass moves on, so order is not kept but nothing stalls. Order only where it matters (within one ticket, not across a tenant), move a row aside after a few attempts with its error kept, and alarm on each tenant's oldest pending age.

[w3] 'Run once' for a digest must be enforced by data, not by the scheduler: before sending, insert a digest row unique on (tenant, recipient, window) and send only when that insert wins, stamping the contributing events with the digest id in the same transaction. It is the discipline the producers already follow, the change and its event committed together.
keyPoints.quote: Create `OutboxEvent` rows in the same transaction as the domain change.

keyPoints.text: [w2] Slower with a small backlog points at what the query steps over: the plan's retry query selects pending or failed rows under an attempt cap and due by a new availableAt column. Rows that exhausted their attempts still sit in the FAILED range the index walks, and availableAt is in no index, so each pass wades through a growing graveyard. Give exhausted rows a status the poller never selects, and index what it filters on.
keyPoints.quote: add `availableAt` to the model and select `status in (PENDING, FAILED) and attempts < 5 and availableAt <= now`

keyPoints.text: [w2] The cleanup does not fight the worker over rows (the worker only ever selects PENDING ones), but one giant DELETE is one giant transaction: a burst of write-ahead log, replica lag, and a long-lived snapshot that holds vacuum back from everything else. Delete in small batches by id at a steady rate, or drop a time partition, and never touch a row that has not reached a final state.

[w2] Lag alarms must follow the lanes: the importer's bulk queue is late by design all evening, so alarm on the age of the oldest interactive row per tenant (the reply topic) and only watch bulk throughput. Topic and tenant are both on every row, so the alarm is a grouped query.

questions.prompt: TRADE-OFF HANDBACK — defend your fairness and lifecycle choices against the alternatives: a queue or table per tenant versus one shared table picked fairly; merging at send time versus accumulating into a scheduled digest; deleting sent rows versus moving them to an archive table versus partitioning by time; suppressing notifications for bulk work versus sending everything at low priority; and equal shares per tenant versus weighted shares. For each, say what you bought, what it cost, and which part of the scenario decided it.

keyPoints.text: [w3] A queue per tenant isolates perfectly and makes each tenant's lag obvious, but 120 queues (and counting) are 120 things to create, poll and watch, and every producer's single atomic insert would have to find the right one. One shared table with a fair pick keeps that single transactional write and costs only an index and a smarter query.

[w3] Merging at send time (the sender folds together whatever is pending for one recipient right now) adds no delay and no new state, but only merges what happens to be queued together; a scheduled digest sends fewer, predictable emails at the cost of delay, a schedule and a per-window sent record to keep it single. A reply to a waiting customer never waits for a digest. Today the sender handles one event at a time.

[w2] Deleting keeps one table but is row-by-row work plus vacuum; an archive table keeps the delivery trail support may need, at the cost of a copy and a delete; time partitions make retention a near-free partition drop, at the cost of the partition key joining every unique key and someone creating next month's partition.

[w2] Sending everything at low priority still emails customers about history and still writes every row; suppressing at the producer saves both, but the suppress switch is a privileged control, and the route-level role gate is applied to only one route in this API (the audit-log read), so the switch needs one of its own.

[w1] Equal shares protect the small tenants and need no data; weighted shares serve a large or paying tenant better but let its flood take more of every pass. The Tenant model has no plan or weight column, so equal shares are what the data supports today.
